analysis.one_liner: Automatically enrolls every child in a Medicare-style public health plan from birth through age 23.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote, drew zero cosponsors in two years, and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create MediKids, a Medicare-style public health plan that automatically enrolls every child at birth and keeps them covered until age 23, no matter what happens with their parents' jobs, income, or where they live. Families with other coverage keep it and pay nothing; families using MediKids pay a modest premium through their tax return, with very low-income families exempt, premiums capped at 5% of income, and out-of-pocket costs above 5% of income refunded as a tax credit. Benefits would include everything Medicaid requires for children plus Medicare-level protections, and long-term costs would be covered by progressive tax increases the Treasury Secretary would have to propose.
analysis.who_benefits: All children born after 2009 would be enrolled automatically at birth and stay covered to 23, through parents' job losses, divorces, and moves — the bill's own findings note more than 9 million uninsured children and say Medicaid and CHIP alone cannot close the gaps. Families get coverage with no cost-sharing for checkups and screenings, reduced cost-sharing at lower incomes, premiums capped at 5% of income, and a refundable credit once out-of-pocket costs pass 5% of family income.

how_it_helps.text: Every child born after 2009 is deemed enrolled in MediKids at birth, with a coverage card issued to the parent, and the safety net re-engages automatically whenever other insurance is lost.

Benefits must include at least Medicare Part A and B coverage, all services Medicaid requires for children (including early screening, diagnostic, and treatment services), and prescription drugs, with no cost-sharing for preventive screenings.

Families with other basic coverage owe no premium; very low-income families (roughly $20,535–$35,195 of income depending on the number of children, adjusted for inflation) are exempt, and no family pays more than 5% of income in premiums.
Cost-sharing is reduced 100%, 75%, or 50% for children in families up to 300% of the poverty line, and a refundable tax credit caps out-of-pocket cost-sharing at 5% of adjusted gross income.

States could not cut Medicaid or CHIP eligibility or benefits for people under 23, and the bill funds pediatric quality measures, a childhood obesity demonstration project, and a model electronic health record format for children.

analysis.who_pays: Families who use MediKids would pay a monthly premium through their tax return, set at one quarter of the program's average per-child cost, waived for very low-income families and capped at 5% of income. General taxpayers would cover start-up costs through transfers to the new MediKids Trust Fund, and the Treasury Secretary would be required to propose a schedule of progressive tax increases to keep the program funded as enrollment grows. Doctors and hospitals would be paid at Medicare-based rates, generally below private insurance rates.

drawbacks.text: Financing was deliberately left half-built: premiums cover only about 25% of the average per-child cost, the Treasury's start-up needs are met by general-fund transfers, and a future Congress would have to pass the progressive tax increases the Treasury Secretary must propose to cover the rest.

Coverage phases in slowly by age group over five years, automatic enrollment applies only to children born after 2009, and coverage ends at 23 — so older uninsured children get nothing for years and everyone ages out into the adult market.

Payment at Medicare-based rates and delivery through Medicare Advantage-style private plans could limit which pediatricians and hospitals participate; the bill itself orders a federal study of children's access to primary and specialty care, an implicit acknowledgment of that risk.

Defenders of private coverage would object that an automatic, cheaper public plan at birth becomes the default whenever private coverage lapses, gradually shifting children out of the private insurance market.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families the upside is concrete: no child loses coverage when a parent changes jobs, and out-of-pocket costs are hard-capped. The honest costs are real: the funding plan was a sketch rather than a finished bill, the phase-in takes five years and ends in a cliff at 23, and Medicare-level payment rates raised a participation question the bill could only order studied. Whether that trade was worth making was never examined — no committee ever held a hearing on it.

outcome.mechanism: Pete Stark introduced it on the first day of the 111th Congress; it was sent to two committees and then to a health subcommittee, where it sat for two years with no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no cosponsors until the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark (D-CA) introduced the MediKids Health Insurance Act on January 6, 2009, the opening day of the 111th Congress, with introductory remarks printed in the Record.
The same day it was referred to two committees, Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means; on January 14 it was referred onward to a health subcommittee.
That was the last recorded action: no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held, and the bill never left committee.
Not a single member of the House — of either party — cosponsored the bill at any point in its two-year life.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and any bill not passed dies with the Congress that introduced it.
The bill aimed at a problem its own findings described: more than 9 million uninsured children, with Medicaid and CHIP leaving gaps during enrollment fluctuations and across state lines.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing arrangement continued unchanged: uninsured children kept relying on Medicaid, CHIP, or whatever their families could find, while families faced no new premium, taxpayers faced no new progressive taxes, and the private child-insurance market faced no public default competitor.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo held; uninsured children gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Fortney Pete Stark
for.what_they_did: Introduced the MediKids bill on the first day of the 111th Congress and delivered introductory remarks; he was the bill's only advocate in the record for two years.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Standing committee, chaired by Rep. Henry Waxman (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral the day it was introduced and passed it to its health subcommittee a week later; the committee never held a hearing or markup.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Standing committee, chaired by Rep. Charles Rangel (D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill under a dual referral on introduction day; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled and the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party in a House where Democrats held 253 of 431 seats, so its only recorded supporter was its Democratic sponsor.

industries.note: MediKids would become the automatic default insurer for children whenever private coverage lapsed, shrinking the market for child-only policies — but the program is required to deliver its benefits through Medicare Advantage-style private plans, sending publicly funded enrollment to insurers, and families with employer coverage keep it and owe no premium.

Guaranteed coverage for every child would reduce uncompensated care, but payments would follow Medicare-style rates that are generally lower than private insurance. The bill itself orders a study of whether enrolled children can actually find primary and specialty providers.
The bill obligates the Treasury Secretary to propose a gradual schedule of progressive tax increases to fund the program as enrollment grows, on top of general-fund transfers during start-up.
